analysis.one_liner: Banned the sale of milk from cows injected with bovine growth hormone for three years.
analysis.headline: The bill never came up for a vote; it died in two House committees when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to sell milk from cows injected with bovine growth hormone (a synthetic copy of a natural cow hormone that boosts milk production) for three years. It would have required anyone selling or injecting the hormone to keep detailed records, imposed fines of up to $10,000 per violation, and ordered the Agriculture Department to study the hormone's effects on cows, on the people who drink the milk, and on farmers' profits.
analysis.who_benefits: Milk drinkers who wanted milk from untreated cows, and dairy farmers who feared the hormone would flood the market with extra milk and drive down the prices they receive. By pausing the hormone for three years, the bill would have kept untreated milk the only milk on store shelves while the government studied the product.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Milk drinkers and small dairy farmers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful, starting six months after enactment, for anyone who knew or should have known to market milk from a cow injected with bovine growth hormone, for a period of three years.
Requires anyone who sells or injects the hormone to keep records of how much they obtained, from whom, and which cows and farmers it went to, so untreated milk could be traced and kept separate.
Sets civil penalties of $1,000 for a first violation and $10,000 for each later one, with each day of illegal sales counted as a separate violation.

Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to study the hormone's direct effects on injected cows, on humans who drink the milk, and on producer profitability, and report to the agriculture committees by January 1, 1993.

analysis.who_pays: The companies developing and selling the hormone would lose three years of sales, and dairy producers who wanted to use it to raise output per cow would forgo that gain during the moratorium. The recordkeeping rules would add paperwork costs for those handling the hormone.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hormone makers and large dairy producers

drawbacks.text: The moratorium would delay a product that raises milk output per cow, which over time can lower production costs and consumer milk prices; farmers and processors bear that cost during the three-year pause.
The bill layers new recordkeeping duties and per-day civil penalties of up to $10,000 on anyone selling or injecting the hormone, a compliance burden on top of an outright sales ban.

It is a temporary ban rather than a safety determination: the required study was to be submitted by January 1, 1993, so the three-year moratorium could expire around the same time without a clear regulatory verdict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded three years of potential efficiency gains in dairy production for a pause that let consumers keep buying untreated milk and let regulators study effects on cows, humans, and farm economics. It was a blunt tool — a flat sales ban plus heavy recordkeeping rather than a labeling or approval standard — but its costs were temporary and fell mostly on the hormone's developers and on producers eager to adopt it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to three subcommittees, none of which acted, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Smith of Vermont introduced the Bovine Growth Hormone Moratorium Act of 1990 in the House on February 7, 1990.
The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced.

Within three weeks it was sent to three subcommittees: Health and the Environment (Energy and Commerce), and Department Operations, Research, and Foreign Agriculture and Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry (Agriculture).
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no markup, no floor vote, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill dead in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies developing bovine growth hormone and the dairy producers hoping to use it were better off, because the moratorium never became law and nothing stood in the way of the hormone reaching the market. Consumers and dairy farmers who wanted untreated milk got no protection from Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hormone developers and large dairy producers

for.name: Rep. Peter Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the moratorium bill in the House on February 7, 1990.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.role: Referred-to committee with jurisdiction over dairy policy
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up; it was sent to a subcommittee and no markup or vote followed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Referred-to committee with jurisdiction over food safety
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never acted; its Health and the Environment Subcommittee took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsored the bill and three Democrats cosponsored it, but no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split shows up in the record.

industries.industry: Animal-health and pharmaceutical makers of bovine growth hormone
industries.note: The bill would have barred sales of milk from hormone-treated cows for three years, cutting off the market for the hormone during that window and requiring detailed records from anyone selling or injecting it. The industry's interest in selling the product ran against consumers who wanted untreated milk and farmers who feared falling milk prices.

industries.industry: Dairy producers who would use the hormone
industries.note: The moratorium would have prevented these producers from raising milk output per cow for three years. Wider hormone use would also have increased total milk supply, which farmers feared would push down the prices all dairy farmers receive.

industries.industry: Dairy farmers generally, especially smaller producers
industries.note: By pausing the hormone, the bill would have delayed a surge in milk supply and helped keep farm milk prices from falling, which matters most to producers without the scale to absorb a price drop.
